content.thinking:
I'm planning to write the whole module carefully in one pass without testing, aiming for an Overwatch-style kraken design: clean bold bio-mech shapes with bevels, panel lines, and a strong accent color against a deep teal/navy body.

I'm settling on indigo-navy body, lighter teal-blue armor plates, cream underside, and glowing orange accents on suckers, rings, and eyes, with dark panel seams on the mantle. For scale, I'm envisioning a giant kraken rising from a water-surface ground plane, mantle around 7m tall with tentacles spanning roughly 14m, built as a skeleton with a central body root, a mantle chain, and eight radial tentacle chains whose tips touch the water line.

I'm adding two longer feeding tentacles with clubs alongside the eight arms, giving ten total tentacle chains of roughly 5-6 joints each (~60 joints total), curving upward then outward then down so the tips sink to the water. I'm also planning a simple foam/water ring lathe disc at the base, sunk slightly below y=0 but within the allowed ground-contact tolerance, and now working out body-facing coordinates with the mantle positioned toward the rear and eyes facing forward.

Now I'm defining the spine chain's catmull-rom points, curving the body upward and backward from a root joint near the hips to a mantle tip around y=6.6-6.9, with the mantle widening near the middle for the head/eye region.

Rethinking the kraken's anatomy: rather than a plain tapering tube, I want a bulbous head around radius 1.3 near y 2.6 with eyes on the sides, and the mantle as an elongated shape extending up and back from there.

I'm figuring out the beak as separate upper and lower jaw pieces attached near where the arms meet at the front underside, roughly at (0, 1.7, 1.0), with a jaw joint for the lower beak so it can open. I also need to nail down the tube's orientation and default roll along the upward-facing path.

Now I'm sketching the body's radius profile along the spine, keying widths at several points from the base skirt through the neck up to the head, mixing circular and slightly elliptical cross-sections.

I'm also second-guessing whether a plain radius taper reads too simple, so I'm thinking about adding color blocking per region, and weighing Overwatch's smooth painted-lit flat shading against a toon/cel approach for the overall material style.

Writing the custom paint function...

Adding seam darkening, then orange chevron accent bands near the mantle, and glowing orange vein strips swept along the dorsal ridge of the mantle and arms for emissive highlights.

For shading, I'll skip complex lighting math since the renderer handles it, instead mottling between two navy tones for a subtle painted texture.

Now I'm planning the body part hierarchy, starting with the spine chain—six joints spanning the catmull curve, resampled and named spine1 through spine6 with a spine role.

Next I'm working out the mantle fins: two triangular fins sweeping outward near the mantle tip, computing the mantle axis direction there and setting up the outline so the fin's outward lateral direction and the mantle's up-back direction define the extrusion plane, with thickness derived from their cross product.

I'll place the fin by sampling the spine path at t=0.82 to get its position, passing that point directly as the attachment coordinate.

For the fin's surface, I'm considering a gradient paint based on position along the fin rather than a stripe.

Now I'm working out the eye placement — two spheres positioned on the sides of the head sphere, checking the geometry so they sit flush on the surface with a slight protrusion, and planning a glowing effect reminiscent of Overwatch-style eyes.

For the brow, I'll skip the extruded armor idea and instead sweep a capsule arc above the eye as a ridge. For the eyeball itself, I'm checking the geometry: a sphere base with a circular iris disc placed flush against its surface, working out the offset so the disc sits properly without floating awkwardly at the edges.

Since placing the circle flush causes issues at the sphere's center, I'm considering using a partial sphere cap (via thetaLength) instead, which stretches the iris texture over just the visible cap region, with the pole oriented along the eye direction axis.

But the polar UV mapping on a cap would distort a planar drawing, so that approach seems too complex. Instead, I think using a decal projected directly onto the eyeball sphere is cleaner—it can map a flat grid texture onto the curved surface at the right position, direction, and size without needing special geometry tricks.

I'm making the iris orange with a dark slit pupil and rim ring, keeping everything outside the iris transparent so the sphere's own sclera-cream color shows through underneath, then applying a glow to the decal so the colors (including the dark pupil and white highlights) read correctly on the eyeball.

For the beak, I'm positioning the jaw joint near the lower-front of the head and working out where the head sphere's surface actually sits at different heights so the beak attaches flush. I'm sketching the upper beak as a hooked, tapering sweep curving forward and downward from the face toward a pointed tip, then starting on the lower beak shape to match.

I'll skip the radula detail but add a plated lip ring torus around the mouth. For the arms—the real stars—I'm planning 8 tentacles rooted around the head at radius ~0.9 from the axis, positioned around y 1.0-1.3 at varying angles.

Each arm's path arcs outward from the body, rises and curves down toward the water, with tip curling up at the surface, and I want variation across arms—different lengths (6-8m) and heights, some rearing up dramatically while others lie lower—to give the kraken a dynamic, flower-like spread when viewed from the front.

I'm working out the vertical curve for each arm using an easing function that rises quickly then settles toward the tip height, making sure resting arms end right at the water's surface with a rounded tip, while raised arms arch upward from the water mound.

I'm now rethinking the pose: the body actually lifts mostly clear of the water while its arms splay outward and drape down, each one touching the surface along its final quarter-length with a slight S-curve sway, and I'm tapering the arm radius from thick at the root to thin at the tip so the resting sections sit naturally without dipping below the waterline.

I'll let the floor contact sink slightly for a small margin of safety. Now I'm thinking about the overall arm choreography—some tentacles should rear up dramatically overhead for a kraken-like silhouette, so I'm sketching a table of arm angles, reach, peak height, tip position, sway, and type, distributing eight arms around the body with the mantle leaning back so arms flow toward the viewer from a front 3/4 angle.

Spacing the arms at roughly 45-degree offsets starting at 22.5 degrees keeps them asymmetric enough to avoid a stiff front/back symmetry while giving each one distinct reach and height values—most lying lower around the base while a couple rise dramatically higher with curling tips for drama, keeping everything within the mantle's overall height.

Now I'm figuring out the two longer feeding tentacles with club-shaped tips—thinking of flaring them outward and upward like horns so they frame the silhouette, but I need to reposition them so their angles don't collide with the arm placements, settling on bringing them closer to the front center instead.

I'm also reconsidering the main arms' spacing—eight arms at 45° offsets starting from front-center—but realizing an arm directly at φ=0 would collide with the beak/mouth location under the head, so I need to raise the beak or shift the arm root positions lower around the skirt to avoid overlap while still keeping the natural ring-around-mouth arrangement cephalopods have.

Good, the arm roots end up buried inside the body at that radius, which works. Now I'm recomputing the spine path with a curved sequence of points rising from the hips through the chest and neck, checking segment lengths along the way.

Now I'm sketching out the body's radius profile along that spine, tapering from a wide head and shoulders down through a narrowing mantle toward the tip.

Settling on roughly 7 m tall with a 16 m arm spread for the kraken, a reasonable monster scale. Now I'm figuring out eye placement on the head surface, using the body sweep's surface function around the head center to position eyes at symmetric azimuth and elevation angles.

I'm making the eyeball sphere protrude from the surface with its gaze direction following the surface normal, giving it that bulging octopus-eye look, then placing an eye decal at that point.

No mirroring needed since the eye is symmetrical. For the eyelid, I'm thinking of using a torus positioned around the eye's equator, sizing its radius to match the sphere's cross-section at that depth so the lid ring hugs the eyeball naturally.

I'll settle the ring at the head's surface, sized to hug the eyeball equator like a socket rim, accepting the slight curvature mismatch as negligible across that width. Now I'm thinking through the brow plate as a half-torus arc positioned over the eye, working out how its rotation aligns with the aim axis so the arc sweeps correctly above the socket.

For colors I'm debating whether to add a thin glowing orange ring inside the socket versus keeping things simpler and skipping it. Then I'm moving to the mantle's dorsal side, planning a row of flattened armor ridge plates spaced along the back surface using frame positions sampled across part of the body length.

Placing dorsal armor plates...

I'm planning glowing orange seam rings as closed loops around the mantle at specific spine joints (around indices 3-5), using the loop's smallest closed path around the body axis at each joint plane, with a thin swept radius for that single accent color.

For the head-neck transition, I'm considering a gorget-style ring of armor plates — maybe a trapezoid plate pattern circling the neck between head and arms, though I want to find a simpler way to define that ring structure than manually specifying each plate.

Checking the arm roots overlap with the collar at that height, which looks fine since the collar sits slightly above. Now verifying the beak doesn't clash with the collar top, estimating where the body surface sits in z near y=2.0 so I can place the mouth correctly, and considering using a surface ray cast instead of manual estimation for accuracy.

I'm defining the beak as a curved sweep with four control points hooking downward from the mouth base, using a tapering radius array so it narrows toward the tip with a rounded end cap.

I'm shaping both upper and lower beak as flattened elliptical sweeps, with the lower beak following a shorter, shallower curve to form the jaw.

Still writing mouth geometry...

Now thinking about suckers on the arms: they sit on the underside, which faces inward when arms curl, so I'll place them using the sweep's position function with an angle offset of 180 degrees to orient toward the belly side rather than the dorsal surface. For raised, curled arms, I want the suckers visible on the inner side facing the viewer.

With roughly 10 arms carrying two rows of suckers and up to 14 per row, I'm worried about part count ballooning past 500 individual sucker meshes, so I'm considering merging sucker geometries by color group to keep the scene performant rather than instantiating each one separately.

Instead I'm realizing cards could solve this: using b.cards with a single sucker texture lets thousands of suckers render as one part while still bending with the skeleton's bones, since cards inherit frame positioning from bones. I'm thinking through a sucker texture design with a cream outer ring and dark center, and how to orient the cards flat against the tentacle surface so they follow the normal correctly.

The flat-card orientation along the surface works geometrically on the curved tube, since the tube's radius is small enough that card edges float just above the surface without clipping. I'm now considering a hybrid approach instead -- using small 3D cone geometry for the cream sucker base plus a flat card just for the dark inner rim, combining dimensionality with efficient rendering.

Deciding to use sticks (individually weighted parts) for suckers so they deform naturally with arm bending, since merged geometries bound to a single bone wouldn't flex with the skin. I'm budgeting part counts: roughly 80 suckers across 8 arms plus 24 on the two feeding clubs, keeping well under the 1000-part limit, with each sucker as a single cylinder shape colored via a paint function based on surface normal.

Thinking through how to distinguish the cap from the side of the cylinder for coloring purposes — normals aren't reliable since stick orientation is arbitrary, and UV coordinates don't cleanly separate cap from side either. I'm considering instead applying a texture to the cylinder, using its cap UV mapping (a disc inscribed in the unit square) to draw a radial sucker pattern with a rim and dark center.

This texture approach gets messy on the side faces though, so I'm abandoning it and considering simpler alternatives: a flat-colored sucker shape, or using a torus (donut) shape to create the rim-with-hole look directly.

A torus ring would naturally read as a sucker rim with the arm's skin visible through the center hole. I'm defining a shared torus geometry, pre-rotated so its axis aligns with the surface normal, scaled appropriately so it can be reused across all sucker placements.

I'm scaling each sucker relative to the local arm radius, embedding it slightly into the surface, and planning two offset rows of suckers along the arm.

For counting the suckers I'm estimating about 12 per row across two rows over ten arms, roughly 240 torus parts total, and checking the triangle budget—opting for a low-segment TorusGeometry to keep the total under 60k triangles while staying under the 1000-object limit.

I'm trimming to 8 arms with 10 suckers per row plus feeding tentacle clubs, landing near 220 parts and about 12k triangles, which fits comfortably. For the tentacle sweeps I'll use 8-sided tubes with adaptive ring counts, keeping each arm cheap at roughly 400 triangles, and then setting up countershading so the arms transition from a dark dorsal navy to a cream-pink belly using angular color sectors.

I'm now defining tip and dorsal coloring: adding orange bands for the tentacle tips as flat accent color, then building a dorsal segment paint function that cycles seam-colored stripes along the arm's length to mimic armor-plate banding.

I'm also estimating texel density for the paint atlas given total arm and body surface area, to make sure thin seam lines stay crisp—settling on a larger paintSize of 2048 for sharper detail.

Now I'm working out the color palette, keeping within the 64 flat-color budget: deep indigo navy tones for the body base and highlights, plus a teal-blue armor accent color.

I'm adding orange as a complementary accent, cream and peach for the underside, and dark navy for shadow areas, with glowing orange tones for eyes/lights -- fitting the Overwatch-style complementary scheme. Now I'm starting to define a function for building the arm chains.

For the arm joints, I'm settling on naming each arm "arm1" through "arm8" with numbered joint segments like arm11..arm16, checking that the naming avoids any collisions across the eight limbs.

I'm deciding the arm chain parents to the spine's root joint (hips), treating each arm as a tentacle-style chain with 6 joints, and computing the path points using a sampled curve across 8 parameter values for a catmull-rom spline.

I'm defining a type for the arm's spec (angle, reach, peak height, tip height, sway, curl), then working out the radius and vertical height functions along the curve parameter so the arms rise, curl inward, and taper toward the tips.

Still tuning arm height curve...

Checking arm root spacing around the body circumference at that radius—eight arms with 0.55 radius each overlap heavily if packed at ring radius 0.9, so I'm testing whether shrinking the root radius to 0.45 still causes crowding, since it still exceeds the available circumference.

Rather than build dedicated webbing between arms, I'll let the collar cover the overlap and just add a slight lateral curl near the tips for the resting arms. For the feeding tentacles, I'm planning two thin long ones with a near-constant radius that bulges into a club shape near the tip, rooted higher on the body between the arms near the mouth, parented to the first spine joint.

The feeding tentacle paths rise and sweep outward toward a peak height before drooping down to the club at the tip, with some hook curl and sway for a hovering, gravitational droop effect using the same spec function but tuned with different peak/tip/hook values. For the clubs themselves, I'm giving them a dense sucker patch in three rows along the inner face, possibly with a glowing orange tip.

Now I'm figuring out the full chain count — eight main arms plus two feeding tentacles, each with six joints, plus the spine and head segments. For sucker placement, I want to distribute them along a portion of each arm's length using clock-angle sectors to mark rows, but I'm realizing that for arms lying flat near the water the suckers would face downward and be hidden, while for the arching, curling arms they'd be more visible — so I need to think about how the sucker-facing angle should vary depending on whether an arm is raised and curled versus resting flat.

I'm settling on placing the belly-colored sector more broadly (around 100° to 260°) with sucker rows positioned near 125° and 235°, right along the edges of that cream band, so they're visible from lower side angles without needing to twist each arm individually. I'm also setting up the sucker geometry as small tori scaled to a fraction of the arm's local radius.

For color, I'm going with a warm peach-cream for the belly and bright orange rims on the suckers so they pop against the body, all handled with one shared material to keep things simple across roughly 220 pieces.

Skipping any logo or emblem decals—instead I'll rely on paint seams, glow bands, dorsal plates, fins, a collar, plated eyes, beak, teeth, and orange-tipped suckers, plus rows of small bioluminescent orange photophore spheres along the sides of the head for extra detail.

I'm placing those glow-sphere rows along both head sides and the mantle flanks, and adding curved armor-plate ribs along the dorsal to break up the scale pattern, while keeping the mantle's underside paler. I'm also sketching a simple lathed water mound as the base for the scene.

The body base sits right at the mound's top so it looks like it's emerging from the water, with the mound tied to the hip root. I'm also considering adding foam rings floating on the water surface around radius 3.3.

For the water itself, I'm weighing whether to extend it into a larger disc, maybe 9 units across, so the arms resting beyond the small mound actually lie on a proper sea surface instead of empty floor.

I'll keep it minimal: a flat disc base, a few thin ripple rings scattered at different radii to suggest motion, and skip extras like droplets or streaming drips since the goal is staging the kraken rising from water, not piling on unnecessary detail.

Checking the overall proportions, the tallest point sits around 6.85 units with fins, and the bounding spread is roughly ±8.5, which looks balanced. The disc base contacts the floor properly, and the arm bottoms stay hidden within the disc shape, so I'll give the disc a radial gradient coloring, darker teal at the center fading lighter toward the edges, to add visual depth without extra geometry.

Mottling the disc with two water tones would eat too much of the paint texture budget given its large surface area, so instead I'll fake the gradient using flat-colored concentric rings, building the disc as stacked lathe tiers that go from deep color at the outer edge to turquoise near the center.

Still defining ring profiles...

I'm attaching the ripple and disc parts to the hips bone, checking that nothing protrudes above the floor bounds, and planning to import the glow helper for the fins and gloss effects.

For the mantle, I'm figuring out how to cap the tapering body with a spike at the tip, orienting it along the path's tangent direction and matching its base radius to the body's end radius for a smooth transition.

Now I'm sketching the body sweep and its paint function, which uses the chain position along the spine and angular degree around the circumference to distinguish dorsal, belly, and seam regions for coloring.

For the layout, I'm thinking through seam rings spaced along the tube using the normalized position along the spine, then defining the mantle's color blocking — darker armor tones on the dorsal edges with ink outlines, mottled navy on the sides, and a lighter ventral belly, mimicking a kraken's natural shading.

Writing paint function logic...

I'm adding a sparse orange accent — a thin racing stripe along the flank seam, plus glow on joint bands, eyes, suckers, and tentacle tips — then writing a similar paint function for the arms using the same distance-based color logic.

Adding sucker placements symmetrically at a=125 with pale cream belly coloring past the seam line, then giving dorsal arms alternating armor-plate segments with a teal stripe near the top. Now I'm adding small bony spikes along the dorsal ridge of each arm near the root for extra texture.

Still placing spikes and cuffs...

Since the joint point sits on the centerline, the plane cut shouldn't miss the surface, so I'll trust the sweep without wrapping it in a try/catch. I'm placing cuff rings at specific joint positions along the arm chain, adjusting the radius slightly at each point, and now tallying up the total part count across body, plates, and spikes.

Setting up imports and tracking which ones I'll actually use...

Defining the color palette for the kraken design...

Now I'm setting up the spine structure, creating a hip joint and a curved spine chain using catmull-rom interpolation through six points, checking whether the chain's role parameter is set up correctly.

Then I'm sweeping the body geometry along the spine with varying radii to form the kraken's tapered form, applying the body color and rounded end caps, followed by generating a surface mesh from the swept body before moving on to defining the eyes.

For each eye side, I'm sampling a hit point on the head surface using azimuth/elevation coordinates, offsetting it slightly outward, and attaching a sclera sphere part positioned at that point and bound to the appropriate spine joint.

Then I'm computing the eye's surface normal to place a decal for the eyeball texture, sizing it to roughly match the eyeball radius with a small lift to avoid z-fighting, and now I'm sketching out the iris/pupil SVG design—thinking through an outer orange ring with a dark outline and a horizontal slit pupil to give it that octopus/kraken look.

Settling on a cream sclera color "#f3d9a4" to give a thin visible ring around the iris, then moving on to defining the lid ring and brow geometry in code.

Writing lid ring code...

Positioning the torus ring at the eye surface level, then placing a brow arc as a bigger concentric torus raised slightly above and outward from the eye socket.

I'm resampling the spine joints by arc length to find the head center near joint index 2. Then I'm computing the jaw/beak position by casting a ray downward to find the skin surface point, falling back to a default location if no hit occurs.

Still writing beak geometry...

Adding teeth as a ring of small cone spikes around the mouth opening, though I'm wary they might clip through the lip torus geometry.

For the collar, I'm figuring out a lathe shape attached near the spine joint, sketching an outline profile of offset points to build the shell-like form.

I'm adjusting the collar's inner and outer radii so it doesn't clip into the body geometry, and checking how it relates to the arm roots positioned below at y=1.0, flaring the collar outward to r=1.65 near y=1.4.

Still working through the arm-collar intersection — lowering the arm root height and recalculating the rise curve so the arms don't visibly pierce through the collar ring.

Checking where the arm actually intersects the collar ring, I realize the arm emergence point overlaps awkwardly with the collar radius—it might look like an armored cuff, which is tolerable but not ideal. I'm considering ditching the large collar in favor of a smaller gorget-style ring placed higher, above where the arms emerge.

But that position collides with the beak, so I'm scrapping the collar lathe entirely and instead planning glowing orange band loops at a few spine joints plus separate armor plate wedges and dorsal plates, along with a head crest made of ridge plates running along the top/back of the head between the eyes.

Still shaping the forehead plate...

Checking the plate-to-head embedding at the edges versus center, it should bulge out at the edges while barely peeking out in the middle, giving a bold cut-plate look. Now I'm planning a thin orange glowing chevron slab layered slightly in front of the shield outline for emphasis.

Next I'm moving to the mantle's dorsal plates, flank photophores, and fins, plus the cream-colored underside near the mantle front. Then I'm sketching a generalized arm-builder structure that defines properties like reach, sway, hook curvature, and root attachment, distinguishing between regular arms and feeder tentacles, with each arm referencing a parent joint from the spine.

Writing arm point generation...

Good, derivative hits zero smoothly at the peak. I'm adding a lateral sway term so the curve isn't flat, then combining direction, side offset, and height into the final position. Now I'm defining the per-arm parameters -- angle, reach, peak height, tip height, sway amount, and hook -- starting with the first arm's spec values.

Checking the front arm's position relative to the beak to make sure it doesn't awkwardly overlap, then continuing to list out specs for the remaining five arms: their angles, reach lengths, peak heights, tip heights, sway, and hook values for curling effects like the rearing arm.

I'm now defining the feeder tentacles separately, positioned at small angles near the beak with their own root position, reach, peak, tip height, outward sway, and hook curl, and checking whether they'd visually clash with the beak or the first couple arms given how close their starting points are to the head's surface.

I shift the feeders to roughly ±32° to keep clearance from the beak and from arm a2's root. I'm also sanity-checking arm a2's trajectory, since it arcs up to a height of 4.6 with a long reach and hook before curling back down near the water, confirming the mid-air arc reads as dramatic rather than physically odd. Then I move into defining the tentacle radius taper function for the arms.

Writing radius function...

Writing the sweep function...

I'm checking whether the floor guard tolerance is enough — if the dip below the sink allowance stays within the small 2% margin, it should be fine, so I'll add a slight buffer to the floor height calculation to keep the arms from poking too far past the disc's bottom edge.

For the suckers, I'm placing them along each arm using the tube's radius at each sample point to scale their size proportionally, looping over two angles (125° and 235°) and generating a set number per row with the sucker geometry built from a small torus rotated to face outward.

The polygon count stays low — a few thousand triangles total across arms and feeders, well within budget. Now I'm working out the feeder clubs, placing their suckers in a few rows near the tips at different angular offsets.

Skipping the glow orb idea for feeder tips in favor of simplicity, giving club suckers a 3x6 row arrangement, and adding dorsal spikes along the arm using cream-colored spike shapes placed at intervals.

I'm placing 5 spikes per arm at increasing positions along its length for an armored look across all 8 arms, around 40 total pieces, then adding orange cuff rings at joints 1 and 3 by sweeping a loop around the arm skin with a small lift and fixed radius.

For the cuffs I'm tuning the ring radius since joint 1 is thicker than joint 3, and adding matching glow sweeps in orange to echo the band colors. I'm also considering a small glowing orange bulb on each arm tip, and planning dorsal mantle plates by sampling frames along the body at uniform intervals, restricted to the back portion past t=0.3.

Writing plate placement code...

Switching to hexagonal plates instead - six-sided cylinders stacked with a smaller top layer, giving that Overwatch-style hex armor look along the dorsal ridge.

Still working out the inset glow placement...

With the plates and insets totaling 18 parts, I'm moving on to the fin geometry — figuring out the extrude directions and computing the cross product to get the correct thickness axis for the fins.

For the fin outline itself, I'm placing it at spine position 0.8 where the mantle radius is about 0.9, then shaping the protruding fin with a sharp tip, making sure the two points at x=0 close properly along the axis.

I'll keep smoothing at 0 for crisp, clean Overwatch-style bevels rather than softening the sharp tip, with a small bevel radius around 0.035 and thickness tapering between 0.12-ish values. For the fin paint function, I'm planning to add an orange tip color based on the x-coordinate extent.

Writing paint shader logic...

I'm placing glowing photophore dots on the mantle and head, then reconsidering their position relative to the orange stripe so they read as beads of light along a seam rather than clashing with the paint.

Working out the spacing math so dots fall symmetrically between seams on both sides, roughly 14 total, and leaving the eye region alone. Now I'm figuring out which spine joints get glowing loop bands around them.

The loops are orange, closed paths with radius around 0.05, placed near joints 1, 3, and 5 along the body, favoring positions between seams for visual balance but allowing slight misalignment since it won't matter much. I'm confirming the loop function accepts a joint frame directly as its anchor and axis reference, and that joint 1 near the head base will correctly wrap just the body surface rather than the head itself.

For the decals and surface queries, eye decals bake onto the body after it's fully formed, and querying the body surface for eye placement happens early enough that later additions don't interfere. I'm also working out the outline typing for the lathe shapes — inline arrays get inferred automatically, but separately declared variables need explicit typing — and checking that the mound's outline coordinates start and end on the axis with no negative x values, while considering how the smoothing parameter will round out the profile.

I'm marking the axis corners of the mound outline as "sharp" so smoothing doesn't distort them, bumping segment count to 20 for a smoother circular profile, and working out how the sea-tier annulus outline overlaps with the mound's edge so the seam between them is covered cleanly.

Now I'm laying out the sea rings as lathed annuli, planning two color tiers—a deep outer band and a lighter inner band—to create concentric ripple-like bands around the central mound.

I'll add white foam tori at key radius boundaries (mound base, tier boundary, outer ripple) for texture, and skip the extra ideas like arm foam rings or water droplets to keep things simple. I'm starting to tally up the total part count for the scene so far.

For the rig, I'm giving the jaw its own joint separate from the spine chain, with the lower beak rigidly attached to it, and I'm positioning the beak and head joints relative to the body's front surface and head joint coordinates—skipping a tongue for simplicity. Now I'm working out the bone hierarchy so the head joint parents the jaw correctly.

Separately, I'm checking that the hips joint can parent the arm chains even though the first arm joint isn't positioned exactly at the hips—confirming this is allowed in the rig structure. I'm also verifying type compatibility details, like making sure number arrays work as point inputs for skinning calls and that the head joint's type correctly satisfies the parent parameter.

Now I'm designing the eye texture, building an SVG with a radial gradient for the iris, a dark outer ring for the sclera edge, and a pupil shape, plus radial lines for added detail. Still writing SVG code...

Generating radial line paths...

I'm checking a ray-cast returns the first hit along a direction near the body center, and verifying the Hit object's position property works correctly. I'm also setting up a lathe-based water/sea mesh using an outline profile attached to the hips bone.

I'm writing an arm paint function that colors the surface based on position along the limb and angle around it—creating seam lines, a belly region, a dorsal ridge stripe, and alternating navy bands based on periodic striping logic.

I'm deciding feeders can reuse the same arm-paint function with a high tip threshold, so club suckers render orange against the cream belly just like the regular arms do, without needing a separate case.

I'm also adding a small glowing sphere at the very tip of the feeder tentacle to act as a bioluminescent lure, sizing it slightly bigger than the tube radius for visual punch, and sketching out the TypeScript type for an Arm spec with fields like reach, peak, tipY, sway, hook, and a feeder flag to distinguish tentacle types.

Checking the path-building logic: using Catmull-Rom splines through Vector3 points for each tentacle chain, resampling by arc length for consistent segment counts, and confirming the sweep function will apply smooth radius tapering with filleted skinning along the curve. I'm also placing sucker details as small embedded stick meshes along the tentacle surface.

I'm verifying the cuff loop geometry around the arm joints—creating a ring-shaped sweep path at the joint location, sizing the tube radius appropriately relative to the arm's thickness, and checking that plain color strings work for the glow material. Now I'm starting the hex plate geometry using a cylinder shape to place along the body surface.

Working out plate placement along the dorsal ridge, computing a scale factor that shrinks the plates as they progress from the head toward the back, and figuring out which side of the tube's local frame faces "up" in world space so the plates sit correctly on the sloped mantle section rather than on the belly side.

That seems backward then — the 0-position might actually mark the front of the mantle, which contradicts the vertical head tube convention where 0 is the back. The reference frame seems to rotate inconsistently across transitions, so I'm not fully confident in this mapping yet.

So the raw reference consistently picks the side agreeing with world up, meaning d=0 is front-facing everywhere along this spine while d=180 is the belly. I want to double-check this against the starting vertical segment to make sure the convention holds there too.

As the path tilts, the up-vector's projection flips toward the front, so the reference angle shifts by π; continuity is maintained by picking whichever π-multiple keeps the angle sequence unbroken, treating the reference as a line rather than a directed vector.

Wait, that actually implies d=180 (back) is the consistent up-facing side everywhere, contradicting my earlier guess — unless the agreement sign flips due to how the reference angle is computed.
